g.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained via next-token prediction: given a
context, predict the probability distribution over the next token.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained via next-token prediction: given a context, predict the probability distribution over the next token.

g.text: This objective teaches the model which tokens tend to appear in which
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) This objective teaches the model which tokens tend to appear in which contexts.

g.text: Fundamentally, it creates a sophisticated pattern-matcher rather than a
system that truly “understands” language or reasoning.
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) Fundamentally, it creates a sophisticated pattern-matcher rather than a system that truly “understands” language or reasoning.

g.text: This pattern-matching nature explains a well-known phenomenon: LLMs are
sensitive to superficial variations in input phrasing.
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) This pattern-matching nature explains a well-known phenomenon: LLMs are sensitive to superficial variations in input phrasing.

g.text: Small changes in wording (Salinas & Morstatter, 2024), question format (Hua
et al., 2025), variable names, or even the order of information (Guan et
al., 2025) can dramatically change model outputs, even when the underlying
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=3) Small changes in wording (Salinas & Morstatter, 2024), question format (Hua et al., 2025), variable names, or even the order of information (Guan et al., 2025) can dramatically change model outputs, even when the underlying problem is semantically identical.

g.text: A model that truly understood would be invariant to such surface-level
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=0) A model that truly understood would be invariant to such surface-level changes; a pattern-matcher is not.

g.text: To bridge the gap between token prediction and problem-solving, researchers
turn to Reinforcement Learning (RL): optimize directly for task success
g.title: N7 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) To bridge the gap between token prediction and problem-solving, researchers turn to Reinforcement Learning (RL): optimize directly for task success rather than next-token likelihood.

g.text: For reasoning tasks like mathematics or coding, rewards can be verified
automatically: the answer is either correct or not.
g.title: N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) For reasoning tasks like mathematics or coding, rewards can be verified automatically: the answer is either correct or not.

g.text: This setting is known as Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
g.title: N9 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) This setting is known as Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (Lambert et al., 2025).

g.text: Among RLVR algorithms, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et
al., 2024) is the most widely used.
g.title: N10 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Among RLVR algorithms, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) is the most widely used.

g.text: While traditional policy gradient methods require a separate value function,
GRPO computes advantages by comparing rollouts within each question group.
g.title: N11 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) While traditional policy gradient methods require a separate value function, GRPO computes advantages by comparing rollouts within each question group.

g.text: The success of DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) demonstrates that this simpler
approach is effective, and GRPO has since been widely adopted for training
g.title: N12 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) The success of DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) demonstrates that this simpler approach is effective, and GRPO has since been widely adopted for training reasoning models.

g.text: The hope is that GRPO will teach the model to “reason better”, to develop
robust problem-solving strategies that generalize beyond the training
g.title: N13 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) The hope is that GRPO will teach the model to “reason better”, to develop robust problem-solving strategies that generalize beyond the training distribution.

g.text: GRPO worsens pattern-matching, not fixes it
In practice, GRPO does not fix the pattern-matching limitation of pretrained
g.title: N14 [Limitation] (cites=0) In practice, GRPO does not fix the pattern-matching limitation of pretrained models; it worsens it.

g.text: (1) Diversity Collapse. GRPO amplifies whatever solution pattern currently
g.title: N15 [Limitation: diversity-collapse] (cites=0) (1) Diversity Collapse. GRPO amplifies whatever solution pattern currently achieves the highest reward.

g.text: If the model has a dominant strategy for a question (e.g., solving
algebraically rather than geometrically), GRPO reinforces this pattern while
starving alternative valid patterns of gradient signal.
g.title: N16 [Limitation: diversity-collapse] (cites=0) If the model has a dominant strategy for a question (e.g., solving algebraically rather than geometrically), GRPO reinforces this pattern while starving alternative valid patterns of gradient signal.

g.text: The result is a model that collapses from knowing multiple solution
strategies to knowing only one (Yue et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Dang
g.title: N17 [Limitation: diversity-collapse] (cites=3) The result is a model that collapses from knowing multiple solution strategies to knowing only one (Yue et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2025).

g.text: This manifests as suboptimal Pass@k performance, the probability of finding
at least one correct answer in k attempts.
g.title: N18 [Limitation: diversity-collapse] (cites=0) This manifests as suboptimal Pass@k performance, the probability of finding at least one correct answer in k attempts.

g.text: Because the model repeatedly produces the same answer rather than exploring
g.title: N19 [Limitation: diversity-collapse] (cites=0) Because the model repeatedly produces the same answer rather than exploring diverse solutions.

g.text: (2) Gradient Diminishing. GRPO’s group-relative normalization creates a
problematic case: when all rollouts for a question receive identical rewards
(all correct or all incorrect), the computed advantages are zero, yielding
g.title: N20 [Limitation: gradient-diminishing] (cites=0) (2) Gradient Diminishing. GRPO’s group-relative normalization creates a problematic case: when all rollouts for a question receive identical rewards (all correct or all incorrect), the computed advantages are zero, yielding no gradient signal.

g.text: Questions that are “too easy” (the model always succeeds) or “too hard” (the
model always fails) contribute nothing to learning.
g.title: N21 [Limitation: gradient-diminishing] (cites=0) Questions that are “too easy” (the model always succeeds) or “too hard” (the model always fails) contribute nothing to learning.

g.text: As shown in Figure 1, over 80% of training questions yield zero gradients
for standard GRPO, with only medium-difficulty questions contributing to
g.title: P22 [Proof] (cites=0) As shown in Figure 1, over 80% of training questions yield zero gradients for standard GRPO, with only medium-difficulty questions contributing to learning.

g.text: root cause: single phrasing per question
The root cause of both failures is that GRPO trains on each question in only
one phrasing, reinforcing a single dominant pattern.
g.title: N23 [Method] (cites=0) The root cause of both failures is that GRPO trains on each question in only one phrasing, reinforcing a single dominant pattern.

g.text: Our insight is simple: present each question in multiple semantically
g.title: N24 [Method] (cites=0) Our insight is simple: present each question in multiple semantically equivalent forms.

g.text: This forces the model to encounter diverse patterns for the same underlying
g.title: N25 [Method] (cites=0) This forces the model to encounter diverse patterns for the same underlying problem, breaking the single-pattern trap.

g.text: We propose transform augmentation: training on multiple phrasings of each
g.title: N26 [Method] (cites=0) We propose transform augmentation: training on multiple phrasings of each question.

g.text: By presenting “What is 2 + 3?”, “Calculate 2+3”, “Find the sum of 2 and 3”,
and “If x = 2+3, what is x?” as variations of the same problem, we expose
the model to diverse solution patterns rather than reinforcing just one.
g.title: N27 [Method] (cites=0) By presenting “What is 2 + 3?”, “Calculate 2+3”, “Find the sum of 2 and 3”, and “If x = 2+3, what is x?” as variations of the same problem, we expose the model to diverse solution patterns rather than reinforcing just one.

g.text: Transform augmentation directly addresses these issues.
g.title: N28 [Method] (cites=0) Transform augmentation directly addresses these issues.

g.text: diverse phrasings → multiple strategies get signal
First, different phrasings trigger different dominant patterns, so
training on diverse phrasings ensures multiple solution strategies
g.title: N28a [Method: mechanism-1] (cites=0) First, different phrasings trigger different dominant patterns, so training on diverse phrasings ensures multiple solution strategies receive gradient signal.

g.text: Second, different phrasings have different difficulty, so grouping
a question with its transforms produces non-zero advantages even
for otherwise “too easy” or “too hard” questions.
g.title: N28b [Method: mechanism-2] (cites=0) Second, different phrasings have different difficulty, so grouping a question with its transforms produces non-zero advantages even for otherwise “too easy” or “too hard” questions.

g.text: Third, training on diverse phrasings reduces the train-test
g.title: N28c [Method: mechanism-3] (cites=0) Third, training on diverse phrasings reduces the train-test distribution shift.

g.text: (Transform-Augmented GRPO), which groups each question with its
transformed variants for joint advantage computation, directly
addressing gradient diminishing while promoting diversity.
g.title: N29 [Contribution] (cites=0) TA-GRPO Algorithm (Section 4): We propose TA-GRPO (Transform-Augmented GRPO), which groups each question with its transformed variants for joint advantage computation, directly addressing gradient diminishing while promoting diversity.

g.text: initialization: it suffices that any transform succeeds; (2)
reduced gradient diminishing: we prove TA-GRPO has lower…
g.title: N30 [Contribution] (cites=0) Theoretical Framework (Section 5): We provide theoretical justification through four mechanisms: (1) non-vacuous initialization: it suffices that any transform succeeds; (2) reduced gradient diminishing: we prove TA-GRPO has lower zero-gradient probability than standard GRPO; (3) a Pinsker-KL generalization bound showing the train-test gap is controlled by KL divergence; and (4) a principled derivation of the pooled advantage formula from Bernoulli variance.

g.text: Pass@k improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. On
competition-level problems (AMC12 and AIME24), TA-GRPO improves
Pass@32 by up to 9.84 points. On…
g.title: N31 [Contribution] (cites=0) Experimental Validation (Section 6): We demonstrate consistent Pass@k improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. On competition-level problems (AMC12 and AIME24), TA-GRPO improves Pass@32 by up to 9.84 points. On out-of-distribution scientific reasoning (GPQA-Diamond), the improvement reaches 5.05 points, confirming the generalization benefits of transform augmentation.
